item.title: Iran names Mojtaba Khamenei as new supreme leader
item.description: Iran's Assembly of Experts has selected Mojtaba Khamenei, the 56-year-old son of the late Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, as the country's new Supreme Leader, according to Reuters and Iranian state media reports on Sunday. The appointment marks the first hereditary transfer of power in the Islamic Republic's history — a system founded in 1979 on the explicit rejection of monarchy.

item.title: Iran war widens as Bahrain reports desalination plant struck, Saudi Arabia sees first deaths
item.description: The war between Iran and a U.S.-Israeli coalition widened into attacks on civilian infrastructure on Sunday as Bahrain accused Iran of striking a desalination plant and Saudi Arabia reported its first fatalities in the nine-day-old conflict.

item.title: Zelenskyy says Ukraine recaptured up to 435 sq km in south
item.description: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced on March 8 that Ukrainian defense forces have recaptured between 400 and 435 square kilometers of territory in southern Ukraine over the past six weeks, calling the campaign a success in disrupting Russian military plans in the region.

item.title: Iran war hits civilian infrastructure as Mojtaba Khamenei named supreme leader
item.description: The nine-day-old war between the U.S.-Israeli coalition and Iran widened into civilian infrastructure on Sunday as both sides struck energy and water facilities, while Iranian state television announced that Mojtaba Khamenei has been named the country's new supreme leader, succeeding his father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed in the opening strikes of the conflict on February 28.

item.title: Energy Secretary Wright says Hormuz tanker traffic could resume within weeks
item.description:
U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said Sunday that an oil tanker had successfully passed through the Strait of Hormuz, offering the first glimmer of hope that the critical waterway could resume regular shipping after being effectively shut down for nearly a week following U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran.

"We're not too long away, I think, before you'll see more regular resumption of ship traffic through the Strait of Hormuz," Wright said on CNN's "State of the Union," adding that in a "worst case" scenario, full resumption could take "a few weeks, that's not months."

item.title: Yardeni raises market meltdown odds to 35% as Iran war widens
item.description:
Veteran Wall Street strategist Ed Yardeni has sharply raised the probability of a market meltdown to 35% for the remainder of 2026, up from 20%, as the escalating war in Iran threatens to upend global energy markets and drag the U.S. economy toward stagflation. In what he described as "fast-moving times," the president of Yardeni Research also slashed his odds of a market meltup, according to Bloomberg.

The revision marks a dramatic shift for one of Wall Street's most closely watched strategists, who just days earlier had maintained his meltdown estimate at 20% while predicting a "short war" scenario that would see oil prices fall quickly once hostilities ended.

item.title: Video shows US Tomahawk missile hitting near Iran school that killed 175
item.description:
Newly released video footage, authenticated by the investigative outlet Bellingcat, shows a US Tomahawk cruise missile striking an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps naval facility in Minab, Iran, on February 28 — the same location where a girls' elementary school was destroyed, killing at least 175 people, most of them children between the ages of 7 and 12.

The footage, originally released by Iran's Mehr News Agency and geolocated by Bellingcat, also captures smoke already rising from the vicinity of the Shajareh Tayyebeh girls' school at the time the missile hits the adjacent IRGC compound. Bellingcat noted that the United States is the only participant in the conflict known to possess Tomahawk missiles, and that Israel does not operate the weapon. The findings add to a growing body of evidence from The New York Times, CNN, CBC, and NPR suggesting the US military was responsible for the deadliest single strike on civilians since the war began on February 28.

item.title: South Korea, Taiwan cap fuel prices as oil tops $100
item.description: South Korea and Taiwan moved on Monday to impose caps on domestic fuel prices as surging oil costs driven by the expanding conflict between the United States, Israel, and Iran ripple through energy-dependent Asian economies.

item.title: Musk pushes vision of robot-powered 'sustainable abundance'
item.description: Elon Musk is doubling down on his vision of a future where artificial intelligence and robots handle all labor, rendering traditional work optional and ushering in an era of what he calls "sustainable abundance." The Tesla CEO's sweeping predictions, repeated across forums from Davos to podcasts in recent months, have drawn both fascination and sharp criticism from economists, politicians, and fellow tech leaders.

item.title: Asian markets plunge as oil tops $100 amid Iran conflict
item.description: A sharp spike in crude oil prices past $100 a barrel sent shockwaves through Asian markets on Monday, with Japanese stocks suffering their steepest single-day decline since April and the Indian rupee sliding to an all-time low as the escalating U.S.-Israel military campaign against Iran continued to choke global energy supplies.

item.title: Microsoft launches Copilot Cowork with Anthropic's Claude for enterprise AI agents
item.description:
Microsoft announced on Sunday a new Copilot Cowork feature built in close collaboration with Anthropic, marking a deepening of the two companies' partnership and the software giant's most aggressive push yet into AI agents for enterprise customers. The feature, part of what Microsoft is calling "Wave 3" of its Microsoft 365 Copilot journey, uses Anthropic's Claude model and the same underlying agentic framework as Anthropic's standalone Claude Cowork product.

Copilot Cowork is designed to handle long-running, multi-step tasks — such as assembling a presentation, pulling together financials, emailing a team, and scheduling prep time — all from a single request. "We really believe right now is an inflection point," Jared Spataro, Microsoft's chief marketing officer for AI at Work, told Fortune. "The inflection point for us is Copilot taking on these agentic capabilities and going from assistance to real doing."

item.title: NATO shoots down second Iranian missile over Turkey in a week
item.description:
NATO air defense systems intercepted a second ballistic missile fired from Iran that entered Turkish airspace on Monday, Turkey's Defense Ministry confirmed, marking the second such incident in less than a week and deepening fears that the broader Middle East conflict could draw in the Western alliance.

The interception occurred at approximately 3:00 PM local time, with debris landing in uninhabited areas of Turkey's southeastern Gaziantep province, according to the ministry's statement. No casualties or injuries were reported. Reuters reported that the ministry emphasized it would "act promptly and decisively as needed" and urged all parties to heed Ankara's warnings.

item.title: Von der Leyen says 'no tears' for Iran regime, drawing EU diplomat backlash
item.description: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen drew sharp criticism from EU diplomats on Monday after she declined to condemn American and Israeli military strikes on Iran and declared that "there should be no tears shed for the Iranian regime" during a speech at the annual EU Ambassadors Conference in Brussels. The remarks deepened an institutional rift over who speaks for Europe on foreign policy as the 10-day-old war in Iran continues to roil the Middle East.

item.title: Trump says ending Iran war will be 'mutual' decision with Netanyahu
item.description: President Donald Trump said Sunday that the decision to end the war with Iran will be made jointly with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, though he indicated he would retain final authority. The remarks, made in a brief phone interview with The Times of Israel, came as Iran formally named Mojtaba Khamenei as its new supreme leader and fighting across the Middle East entered its tenth day.

item.title: Wall Street slides as Iran conflict sparks oil surge
item.description:
U.S. stock markets opened with steep losses on Monday as crude oil prices surged above $110 per barrel for the first time since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022, deepening fears that the widening conflict in the Middle East will choke global energy supplies and tip the economy toward stagflation.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average, S&P 500, and Nasdaq Composite all fell sharply at the open, extending a punishing stretch that has dragged major indices lower since their January highs. Futures had pointed to losses of roughly 1.5% before the opening bell. The selling followed a brutal week on Wall Street, with the Dow closing Friday at 47,502 after dropping nearly 1% in that session alone.

item.title: Study finds satellite radar warming could cut high-risk bridge counts by a third
item.description: A global study of 744 long-span bridges has found that structures in North America face the highest risk of geo-hazard-related damage anywhere on Earth, with many built during a 1960s construction boom now nearing or surpassing their intended lifespans. The research, published this week in Nature Communications, proposes satellite radar imaging as a tool to monitor aging infrastructure and reduce the number of bridges classified as high risk.

item.title: NATO intercepts second Iranian missile in Turkish airspace
item.description:
NATO air defense systems shot down a second Iranian ballistic missile in Turkish airspace on Monday, the Turkish Ministry of National Defense confirmed, as debris rained down on uninhabited fields in the southeastern province of Gaziantep. The interception, which occurred at approximately 3:00 p.m. local time, marks the second such incident in five days and deepens a crisis that has drawn the Western alliance closer to direct involvement in the widening U.S.-Iran conflict.

Hours later, the U.S. State Department ordered non-emergency government employees and their families to leave the American consulate in Adana, near the strategic Incirlik Air Base, citing safety risks. Americans in southeastern Turkey were "strongly encouraged to depart now," the department said in an updated travel advisory.

item.title: UN chief to argue Iran war bolsters case for renewables
item.description:
As the U.S.-Israeli air campaign against Iran enters its second week, the conflict's disruption to global fossil fuel supplies has intensified a debate over whether the crisis could accelerate the world's transition to renewable energy. With approximately 20% of global crude oil and natural gas supply suspended and oil prices climbing to their highest levels since 2022, energy experts, world leaders, and industry groups are making the case that homegrown clean power is not just a climate imperative but a matter of national security.

U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres plans to press that argument on Monday. "The turmoil we are witnessing today in the Middle East makes it evident that we are facing a global energy system largely tied to fossil fuels — where supply is concentrated in a few regions and every conflict risks sending shock waves through the global economy," Guterres said in an email to The Associated Press. "In past oil shocks, countries had little choice but to absorb the pain. Now they have an exit ramp."

item.title: G7 fails to agree on oil reserve release as crude tops $100
item.description:
Finance ministers from the Group of Seven nations held an emergency call Monday morning to discuss the historic surge in oil prices but failed to reach consensus on a joint release of strategic petroleum reserves, with France saying the bloc is "not there yet" on organizing a global drawdown.

French Finance Minister Roland Lescure made the remarks after the virtual meeting, according to Bloomberg, which reported that the G7 is "not there yet" in terms of a coordinated release of emergency oil inventories despite the escalating crisis triggered by the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.

item.title: Greek tanker exits Hormuz with Saudi crude as traffic slowly resumes
item.description:
A Greek-operated oil tanker carrying a million barrels of Saudi crude has become one of the first large vessels to exit the Persian Gulf since the Strait of Hormuz was effectively shut down by Iranian attacks more than a week ago, according to Bloomberg, even as the vast majority of shipping operators remain unwilling to risk the passage.

The Shenlong, operated by Greece's Dynacom Tankers Management Ltd., switched off its transponder in the Persian Gulf on March 4 while heading toward Hormuz and began signaling again off the coast of India on Monday morning, ship-tracking data compiled by Bloomberg showed. U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright confirmed the transit in a weekend interview with Fox News, and told CNN that a broader resumption of traffic was "not too long away," adding that the worst-case timeline was "a few weeks, that's not months".
